correct_answer.text: Pilot reports can provide the most valuable information on any weather hazards, including turbulence, that is useful to other pilots approaching the same area.

explanation: Pilot reports (AIREPs or PIREPs) are real-time observations from aircraft that have just flown through the area. They are the most current information on actual turbulence.

question: In which conditions is the turbulence the worst at 2 000 ft?

options.label: A
options.text: With katabatic winds.

options.label: B
options.text: When the ambient pressure is very low.

options.label: C
options.text: Strong winds and rough terrain.

options.label: D
options.text: Rough terrain and a clear warm night.

correct_answer.text: Strong winds and rough terrain.

explanation: At 2 000 ft the worst turbulence is mechanical: strong winds over rough or mountainous terrain create large eddies throughout the low levels.

question: Which option is true about mountain waves?

options.label: A
options.text: In a mountain-wave system at medium to high level the smooth outline of any associated cloud indicates that turbulence and strong vertical currents are NOT likely to be present.

options.label: B
options.text: Mountain waves tend to occur at low level, where the wave motion is severely weakened by the terrain and therefore the wave flow is NOT likely to be a hazard to aircraft.

options.label: C
options.text: The airflow in a mountain-wave system is often smooth but vertical currents can be strong enough to exceed the performance capability of an aircraft.

options.label: D
options.text: For an aircraft entering in a mountain-wave system, the most likely hazard in the wave flow is severe turbulence in the area upwind of the mountain range.

correct_answer.text: The airflow in a mountain-wave system is often smooth but vertical currents can be strong enough to exceed the performance capability of an aircraft.

explanation: Airflow in a wave is often laminar and smooth (lenticular cloud with smooth edges), but the up and down currents can reach thousands of ft/min, exceeding the aircraft's climb or descent performance. Rotors underneath are very turbulent.

question: The average position of the polar front in the northern hemisphere is:

options.label: A
options.text: located near 65°N during the whole year.

options.label: B
options.text: more southerly during the summer than during the winter.

options.label: C
options.text: located near 55°N during the whole year.

options.label: D
options.text: more southerly during the winter than during the summer.

correct_answer.text: more southerly during the winter than during the summer.

explanation: The polar front follows the sun. In winter, cold polar air extends further south, so the front lies further south (about 30–40°N). In summer it retreats north (about 50–60°N).

question: An aircraft is parked outside and the crew arrives to the aircraft for an early morning flight. Since the night was clear and freezing cold, what is the crew likely to observe on the aircraft?

options.label: A
options.text: The sub-zero air temperature has probably created supercooled water droplets, which have formed clear ice on the aircraft.

options.label: B
options.text: The overnight radiative cooling of the land and fuselage surface may have caused hoar frost to form, covering the aircraft.

options.label: C
options.text: The convective cooling of the surface air sitting on the land overnight could lead to vapour sublimation on the fuselage.

options.label: D
options.text: The aircraft is likely to be covered in a hard layer of rime ice due to vapour sublimation.

correct_answer.text: The overnight radiative cooling of the land and fuselage surface may have caused hoar frost to form, covering the aircraft.

explanation: On a clear, cold night the aircraft surfaces cool by radiation below the frost point. Water vapour deposits directly as ice crystals, forming hoar frost over the aircraft, which must be removed before flight.

question: Given that all other variables remain constant, what happens to the base of a free convective cloud?

options.label: A
options.text: It will rise with increasing temperature at the Earth’s surface.

options.label: B
options.text: It will lower with decreasing pressure at the Earth’s surface.

options.label: C
options.text: It will lower with increasing wind speed at the Earth’s surface.

options.label: D
options.text: It will rise with increasing mixing ratio at the Earth’s surface.

correct_answer.text: It will rise with increasing temperature at the Earth’s surface.

explanation: The convective cloud base is roughly the height where the rising thermal cools to its dew point (≈ 400 ft × temperature–dew point spread). A higher surface temperature with the same dew point increases the spread, so the base rises.

question: A pre-flight weather briefing must be prepared, and information is needed on the expected weather at the destination for an arrival approximately 3 hours later. Which of the following, available from meteorological services during flight planning, can provide this information? (1)  The TAF covering the estimated time of arrival. (2)  The current ATIS message promulgated by the destination airport. (3)  NOTAMS in force at the estimated time of arrival. (4)  The latest METAR (giving particular scrutiny to any trend information). (5)  Aerodrome warnings in force at the estimated time of arrival. (6)  The current VOLMET information promulgated by the destination airport. (7)  The Significant Weather Chart covering the area of the destination airport valid at the estimated time of arrival. (8)  Relevant SIGMET information valid at the estimated time of arrival.
explanation: For an arrival 3 hours later, you need forecasts: TAF, METAR with TREND, aerodrome warnings, SIGWX chart and SIGMETs valid at the ETA. ATIS and VOLMET give current weather only, and NOTAMs are not meteorological information.

question: Mountain waves create rotors in the air. If you compare the height of the rotor to the mountain top, it can be said that the center of the first rotor is ...

options.label: A
options.text: just above the inversion layer in the valley.

options.label: B
options.text: much lower down slope on the windward side of the mountain.

options.label: C
options.text: at the same height or just below the top of the mountain on the leeward side.

options.label: D
options.text: much higher than the top of the mountain ridge on the leeward side.

correct_answer.text: at the same height or just below the top of the mountain on the leeward side.

explanation: The first rotor forms beneath the first wave crest in the lee. Its centre is typically at about ridge-top height or a little below it, on the lee side.

question: Which of the following statements about mixed or cloudy ice it true?

options.label: A
options.text: It forms when frozen surface heats up and the ice starts to melt.

options.label: B
options.text: It is the least commonly type of ice encountered.

options.label: C
options.text: It forms when relatively small hail stones accumulate on a warm surface.

options.label: D
options.text: It forms in conditions between the ideal conditions for clear ice and rime ice.

correct_answer.text: It forms in conditions between the ideal conditions for clear ice and rime ice.

explanation: Mixed (cloudy) ice is a mix of clear and rime ice. It forms in conditions between those favouring clear ice (large drops, near 0 °C) and rime (small drops, colder temperatures), such as in cumuliform cloud with varying drop sizes.

question: Refer to figure 050-13. Assuming the usual direction of movement, to which position will the polar frontal wave have moved (after a certain time)? Figure 050-13

options.label: A
options.text: Position 3.

options.label: B
options.text: Position 2.

options.label: C
options.text: Position 1.

options.label: D
options.text: Position 4.

correct_answer.text: Position 3.

explanation: A polar-front wave normally moves in the direction of the warm-sector isobars, generally eastwards (NE) in the NH. In the figure that corresponds to position 3.

question: The sinking of air most often happens...

options.label: A
options.text: in areas with high atmospheric humidity.

options.label: B
options.text: if a cold air mass is located above a warmer ground.

options.label: C
options.text: in high pressure areas.

options.label: D
options.text: at cold fronts.

correct_answer.text: in high pressure areas.

explanation: Subsidence (sinking of air) is typical of high-pressure areas. Air converges aloft, sinks, warms adiabatically and diverges at the surface.

question: Refer to figure 050-184. Which of these pressure systems is shown by "J" in the figure? The figure shows Southern Hemisphere.

options.label: A
options.text: Blocking anticyclone

options.label: B
options.text: Frontal anticyclone

options.label: C
options.text: Frontal depression

options.label: D
options.text: Trough

correct_answer.text: Frontal depression

explanation: In the Southern Hemisphere, low-pressure systems rotate clockwise and the fronts are mirror images of the NH pattern. 'J' is a closed low with associated fronts, which makes it a frontal depression.

question: How are area forecasts of upper-air meteorological phenomena for flight planning purposes produced?

options.label: A
options.text: Each State's Meteorological Office gathers information independently and produces upper-air gridded forecasts for departing aircraft.

options.label: B
options.text: Every ICAO Region has its own Weather Area Flight Centre, which provides forecasts for all aircraft departing from the Region.

options.label: C
options.text: Every State has its own Weather Area Flight Commission, which provides forecasts for all aircraft registered in that State.

options.label: D
options.text: The responsible World Area Forecast Centre provides gridded data of forecast upper-air phenomena including winds, icing, and turbulence.

correct_answer.text: The responsible World Area Forecast Centre provides gridded data of forecast upper-air phenomena including winds, icing, and turbulence.

explanation: The World Area Forecast System (WAFS) produces upper-air forecasts. The WAFCs in London and Washington issue global gridded data (winds, temperature, humidity, icing, turbulence, CB) and SIGWX for flight planning.

question: Check the correctness of the following statements: (1) The summer monsoon in the southern part of India is a NE monsoon. (2) The prevailing climatic zone in Australia is the dry climate.

options.label: A
options.text: 1 is correct, 2 is not correct.

options.label: B
options.text: 1 and 2 are not correct.

options.label: C
options.text: 1 is not correct, 2 is correct.

options.label: D
options.text: 1 and 2 are correct.

correct_answer.text: 1 is not correct, 2 is correct.

explanation: (1) is wrong: the summer monsoon over southern India is a SW monsoon, and the NE monsoon is the winter one. (2) is right: most of Australia has an arid or semi-arid (dry) climate.

question: Refer to figure 050-138. Where do you encounter the greatest headwind when flying at a low altitude?

options.label: A
options.text: At position 3

options.label: B
options.text: At position 4

options.label: C
options.text: At position 1

options.label: D
options.text: At position 2

correct_answer.text: At position 4

explanation: At low level the headwind is strongest where the pressure gradient is steepest (isobars closest together) and the geostrophic wind blows most directly against your track. In figure 050-138 that is position 4.

question: Fog can form when the temperature of air is in contact with a colder surface and the temperature drops below its dew point. Which type of inversion is responsible for this?

options.label: A
options.text: Frontal inversion

options.label: B
options.text: Turbulence inversion

options.label: C
options.text: Ground inversion

options.label: D
options.text: Subsidence inversion

correct_answer.text: Ground inversion

explanation: When air is cooled from below by a cold surface (radiation or advection over cold ground), the temperature increases with height from the surface. That is a ground (surface) inversion, which traps moisture and allows fog to form.

question: What is the most reliable source of information for a pilot looking to avoid areas of potentially dangerous turbulence?

options.label: A
options.text: ADS-B package of weather information.

options.label: B
options.text: By requesting and listening to reports from pilots that have recently been flying in the same area and experienced CAT (PIREPs or SIGMETs).

options.label: C
options.text: Satellite images and broadcast, and remote sensing from satellites in turbulence mode.

options.label: D
options.text: Information from meteorological (weather) balloon ascents.

correct_answer.text: By requesting and listening to reports from pilots that have recently been flying in the same area and experienced CAT (PIREPs or SIGMETs).

explanation: Reports from aircraft that have just flown through the area (PIREPs and AIREPs, and SIGMETs based on them) are the most reliable indication of actual turbulence, especially CAT, which is otherwise invisible.

question: How does the air temperature affect the dew point temperature?

options.label: A
options.text: The dew point decreases as soon as the temperature falls below the current dew point at a constant pressure.

options.label: B
options.text: Air can hold a larger amount of water as soon as the temperature increases. This causes the dew point to increase, too.

options.label: C
options.text: The outside air temperature has no effect on the dew point, but can change the relative humidity within the atmosphere.

options.label: D
options.text: The dew point is inversely proportional to the outside air temperature.

correct_answer.text: The dew point decreases as soon as the temperature falls below the current dew point at a constant pressure.

explanation: The dew point can't exceed the air temperature. If the air cools below its current dew point, water vapour condenses out, the moisture content falls, and the dew point drops along with the temperature.

question: Refer to figure 050-25. What temperature change can be expected when the cold front is approaching position B?

options.label: A
options.text: A drop in temperature.

options.label: B
options.text: Approximately constant temperature.

options.label: C
options.text: A rise in temperature.

options.label: D
options.text: Irregular temperature fluctuations.

correct_answer.text: Approximately constant temperature.

explanation: Position B in figure 050-25 is in the warm sector. Temperature there stays roughly constant until the cold front actually passes, then it drops.

question: Consider a low-pressure system at the surface, and a high-pressure system in the upper air. A vertical cross-section of isobaric surfaces will show isobars curved.

options.label: A
options.text: Upwards at the surface, and downwards in the upper air.

options.label: B
options.text: Downwards at any altitude.

options.label: C
options.text: Downwards at the surface, and upwards in the upper air.

options.label: D
options.text: Upwards at any altitude.

correct_answer.text: Downwards at the surface, and upwards in the upper air.

explanation: Low pressure at the surface makes the isobaric surfaces dip downwards there. A high aloft makes them bulge upwards at upper levels.

question: Refer to figure 050-25 What wind direction will likely prevail at point "B"?

options.label: A
options.text: Southeast

options.label: B
options.text: Southwest

options.label: C
options.text: East

options.label: D
options.text: Northwest

correct_answer.text: Southwest

explanation: Position B in figure 050-25 is in the warm sector of a NH depression, where the wind is typically south-westerly (between the warm front and the cold front).

question: Refer to figure 050-239 An aircraft is planned to fly from A (20N105E) to B (08S110E). The track follows the straight line shown in the chart and the aircraft’s cruising FL changes halfway from the initial FL350 to FL300. Given the above, where along the route would you expect a high concentration of hazardous ice crystals?

options.label: A
options.text: At cruising altitude for the first 600 NM after initial climb.

options.label: B
options.text: Clear for the first 800 NM or so and then likely for the rest of the cruise.

options.label: C
options.text: At cruising altitude for the last 200 NM before descent.

options.label: D
options.text: It is NOT expected to encounter a high concentration at cruising altitude on this route.

correct_answer.text: Clear for the first 800 NM or so and then likely for the rest of the cruise.

explanation: The southern part of the route crosses the equatorial convective zone (ITCZ), with deep CBs and high concentrations of ice crystals at cruise levels. The northern part (about the first 800 NM) is clear of it.

question: What are the units of measurement used for RVR?

options.label: A
options.text: Feet (ft) only

options.label: B
options.text: Meters (m) or feet (ft) at discretion of State

options.label: C
options.text: Kilometres (km) only

options.label: D
options.text: Meters (m) or feet (ft) at discretion of ATC

correct_answer.text: Meters (m) or feet (ft) at discretion of of State

explanation: In this question bank's answer, RVR may be reported in metres or feet at ATC's discretion. In practice, ICAO and Europe report RVR in metres, while the US uses feet.

question: A pilot flies from the East towards a stable front approaching from the West. What changes in the weather should the pilot expect?

options.label: A
options.text: At approximately 800 km ahead of the surface front there is overcast cirrostratus the cloud base lowers to become a typical overcast altostratus and finally a nimbostratus. At approximately 300 km ahead of the surface front, the aircraft encounters rain which eases.

options.label: B
options.text: At approximately 800 km ahead of the surface front there is overcast cirrostratus the cloud base lowers to become a typical overcast altostratus and finally a nimbostratus. At approximately 300 km ahead of the surface front, the aircraft encounters rain which intensifies.

options.label: C
options.text: Flying towards the surface front, the aircraft suddenly encounters an area with a low cloud ceiling and rain, then conditions improve on the course to the West until the rain finally ceases. The cloud ceiling rises slowly, at a distance of approximately 800 km from the surface front, the sky clears.

options.label: D
options.text: At approximately 800 km ahead of the surface front there is overcast cirrostratus the cloud base lowers to become a typical overcast altostratus and finally a cumulonimbus. At approximately 300 km ahead of the surface front, the aircraft encounters rain which intensifies.

correct_answer.text: At approximately 800 km ahead of the surface front there is overcast cirrostratus the cloud base lowers to become a typical overcast altostratus and finally a nimbostratus. At approximately 300 km ahead of the surface front, the aircraft encounters rain which intensifies.

explanation: A stable warm-front type sequence: about 800 km ahead you meet CI/CS, then the base lowers through AS to NS. About 300 km ahead, continuous precipitation starts and becomes heavier as you near the surface front.

question: Which of the following will dissipate orographic fog?

options.label: A
options.text: Anabatic wind

options.label: B
options.text: Adiabatic cooling

options.label: C
options.text: Downslope wind

options.label: D
options.text: Upslope wind

correct_answer.text: Downslope wind

explanation: Orographic (hill) fog forms when moist air is forced up a slope and cools to its dew point. A downslope wind warms the air adiabatically and dissipates it.

question: You are flying towards an aerodrome west of a mountain ridge. Cumuliform clouds are at the height of the top of the ridge overhead the aerodrome. Wind is coming from the west and the zero- degree isotherm aligns with the height of the ridge. Where would you expect the highest risk of aircraft icing?

options.label: A
options.text: On the Western side of the ridge, halfway up its slope.

options.label: B
options.text: On the Western side of the ridge, at the same height as the ridge.

options.label: C
options.text: On the Eastern side of the ridge, halfway up its slope.

options.label: D
options.text: On the Eastern side of the ridge, at the same height as the ridge.

correct_answer.text: On the Western side of the ridge, at the same height as the ridge.

explanation: With a westerly wind, the western (windward) side of the ridge has forced ascent, adding lift and liquid water to the cumuliform cloud. The highest icing risk is on the windward side where the cloud is at or just above the freezing level, at ridge height.

question: From the below, choose the statement correctly describing the formation of cold-air drop.

options.label: A
options.text: A cold-air drop is formed when a large low-pressure centre is created above the surface descent of very cold air within a warm anticyclone.

options.label: B
options.text: Air behind a slow-moving warm front passes over a cold surface. In this case the cooling of the air above can result in a localised pool of cold air forming, and a corresponding fall in pressure. This is known as a cold-air drop.

options.label: C
options.text: A large mass of polar air moves to a lower latitude and becomes surrounded by warmer air. This creates a low-pressure centre above the surface, known as cold-air drop.

options.label: D
options.text: In summer, the air behind a cold front can slow down as the primary system becomes weaker. In this case surface heating results in a fall in pressure, which creates a small area of lower pressure known as a cold-air drop.

correct_answer.text: A large mass of polar air moves to a lower latitude and becomes surrounded by warmer air. This creates a low-pressure centre above the surface, known as cold-air drop.

explanation: A cold-air drop forms when a mass of polar or arctic air is cut off and moves to lower latitudes, becoming surrounded by warmer air. This creates an isolated cold low aloft, often with little surface signature.

question: An aircraft flies at FL190 from London to South France and experiences a strong wind from the left. Which of the following is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The true altitude remains constant.

options.label: B
options.text: The radio altimeter shows a climb.

options.label: C
options.text: The true altitude will decrease.

options.label: D
options.text: The true altitude will increase.

correct_answer.text: The true altitude will decrease.

explanation: Flying south from London with a strong wind from the left (from the east), in the NH Buys Ballot's law puts low pressure to the south, ahead of you. At constant FL you are flying into lower pressure (and colder air), so true altitude decreases: 'high to low, look out below'.

question: The condensation process in the atmosphere is initiated by:

options.label: A
options.text: Daily atmospheric pressure variations.

options.label: B
options.text: Micrometric solid and liquid particles.

options.label: C
options.text: Gaseous carbon-dioxide molecules.

options.label: D
options.text: High-frequency electromagnetic waves.

correct_answer.text: Micrometric solid and liquid particles.

explanation: Condensation needs condensation nuclei: microscopic solid and liquid particles such as salt, dust, smoke and sulphates, on which water vapour condenses.

question: The type of information given by a ground weather radar is a map with an indication of:

options.label: A
options.text: Precipitation/Obscuration and meteorological visibility

options.label: B
options.text: Precipitation and its intensity

options.label: C
options.text: Obscuration and fog

options.label: D
options.text: Precipitation and fog

correct_answer.text: Precipitation and its intensity

explanation: Ground weather radar detects precipitation-sized particles and displays where precipitation is and how intense it is. It does not show fog or visibility.

question: Refer to figure 050-62. Refer to the jet stream section overhead Iceland. In this part of the jet stream there are two small, solid black lines across the jet stream axis. Which of the following correctly decodes this symbol?

options.label: A
options.text: There is insufficient space in that area of the chart to describe the significant weather associated with the jet stream.

options.label: B
options.text: The height of the jet stream axis changes by +/- 3 000 ft and / or the speed varies by +/- 20 kt.

options.label: C
options.text: It indicates that the jet stream is rapidly decaying.

options.label: D
options.text: The height of the jet stream axis changes by +/- 6 000 ft and / or the speed varies by +/- 30 kt.

correct_answer.text: The height of the jet stream axis changes by +/- 3 000 ft and / or the speed varies by +/- 20 kt.

explanation: On a SIGWX chart, a double bar across the jet axis marks a change of 20 kt in jet speed and/or 3 000 ft in the jet core height.

question: Refer to figure 050-123. In the Northern Hemisphere, an aircraft flies from A to B:

options.label: A
options.text: Wind: Decreasing, backing.

options.label: B
options.text: Wind: Increasing, backing.

options.label: C
options.text: Wind: Increasing, veering.

options.label: D
options.text: Wind: Decreasing, veering.

correct_answer.text: Wind: Increasing, veering.

explanation: Wind strength depends on isobar spacing (closer means stronger), and in the NH the wind veers (turns clockwise) as you cross a trough or front. Flying from A to B in figure 050-123 the wind increases and veers.

question: What would be a dangerous mistake while observing icing in flight?

options.label: A
options.text: Informing ATC about the icing conditions mentioning the levels between icing conditions were experienced.

options.label: B
options.text: Descending to a different flight level where icing conditions are not suspected.

options.label: C
options.text: Thinking the hoar frost appears to not affect the aerodynamic shape of the wing.

options.label: D
options.text: Ice protection systems are selected ON.

correct_answer.text: Thinking the hoar frost appears to not affect the aerodynamic shape of the wing.

explanation: Even thin hoar frost roughens the wing surface, which reduces lift and increases stall speed. Assuming it doesn't affect the wing is dangerous, so frost must always be removed before flight.

question: Which cloud species is described by the following definition? "Clouds which present, in at least some portion of their upper part, cumuliform protuberances in the form of turrets which generally give the clouds a crenellated appearance. The turrets, some of which are taller than they are wide, are connected by a common base and seem to be arranged in lines. The typical character is especially evident when the clouds are seen from the side."

options.label: A
options.text: Fractus

options.label: B
options.text: Calvus

options.label: C
options.text: Castellanus

options.label: D
options.text: Congestus

correct_answer.text: Castellanus

explanation: Castellanus clouds have turret-like, crenellated towers rising from a common base, often in lines. Seen in the morning (e.g. ACC), they indicate mid-level instability and possible thunderstorms later.

question: Which of the following statements are correct? (1) In a mixed cloud the ice crystals grow at the expense of supercooled water droplets. (2) In the mid-latitudes heavy rain showers are only formed by the coalescence process.

options.label: A
options.text: None

options.label: B
options.text: 2 only

options.label: C
options.text: 1 and 2

options.label: D
options.text: 1 only

correct_answer.text: 1 only

explanation: (1) is true: in a mixed cloud the ice crystals grow at the expense of the supercooled droplets, because saturation vapour pressure over ice is lower (Bergeron–Findeisen process). (2) is false: in the mid-latitudes heavy showers mainly come from the Bergeron (ice) process, and coalescence dominates mainly in warm tropical clouds.

question: What are the properties of a continental air mass?

options.label: A
options.text: Wet, but it loses moisture while travelling over land.

options.label: B
options.text: Wet, but it adds moisture due to the stable weather conditions overhead land surfaces.

options.label: C
options.text: Dry, because it loses moisture while travelling over land.

options.label: D
options.text: Dry, but it adds moisture due to stable weather conditions overhead land surfaces.

correct_answer.text: Dry, because it loses moisture while travelling over land.

explanation: A continental air mass forms over land. It is dry because it has no water source to draw moisture from, and it loses moisture over land.

question: When a cold front has to cross a chain of mountains, its activity:

options.label: A
options.text: decreases when it reaches the mountains.

options.label: B
options.text: strengthens "upwind" of the mountains.

options.label: C
options.text: ceases immediately.

options.label: D
options.text: is not disturbed by the mountains.

correct_answer.text: strengthens "upwind" of the mountains.

explanation: When a cold front meets a mountain range, the extra forced ascent upwind (windward) of the range strengthens its activity. On the lee side, descent weakens it.

question: How often is a wind shear report updated? Every...

options.label: A
options.text: 15 min

options.label: B
options.text: 1 hour

options.label: C
options.text: 1 sec

options.label: D
options.text: 1 min

correct_answer.text: 1 min

explanation: Wind shear warnings from a LLWAS or similar are based on continuously monitored anemometers and are updated about every minute.

question: An aircraft on approach received an alert from the Low Level Wind Shear Alerting System (LLWSAS), which is followed by information from an ATC saying: "Wind shear alert, centre-field wind 150 at 12, north-east boundary wind 060 at 25." How should you interpret this message? Note: The centre-field wind is obtained from an anemometer, which is located in the middle of the airfield, and the north-east boundary wind is obtained from a different anemometer near that location.

options.label: A
options.text: A weak warm front is passing the airfield, causing a shift in wind direction and speed.

options.label: B
options.text: An active anticyclone over the airfield is causing a marked backing of the wind from centre field to the boundary.

options.label: C
options.text: The change in wind direction and speed may indicate an active downburst.

options.label: D
options.text: A cold front moving east is causing a marked veering of the wind from centre field to the boundary.

correct_answer.text: The change in wind direction and speed may indicate an active downburst.

explanation: The centre-field wind is 150/12 and the NE boundary wind is 060/25, which is a large change in direction and speed over a short distance. That pattern of outflow from a single point is typical of an active downburst or microburst.

question: You are planning a flight in Western Europe and your destination aerodrome, with an elevation of 700 ft (AMSL), is located inland, on a crest of a small ridge. Before commencing the flight, you are checking the actual weather at your destination and receive the following METAR: 0850Z 27015KT 0100 R29/0650 FG VV/// 03/03 Q1005 A second aerodrome is located a bit lower, at 200 ft (AMSL), and just a few miles west from your destination, and reports the following METAR: 0850Z 26011KT 9999 SCT0500 05/03 Q1005 Given the information above, what type of fog can you expect at the destination aerodrome and which of the options correctly describes the fog’s dissipation?

options.label: A
options.text: Advection fog can be expected, and a change in the air mass is required to dissipate the fog.

options.label: B
options.text: Orographic fog can be expected, and as the temperature rises with diurnal heating, the fog is likely to lift into a cloud.

options.label: C
options.text: Radiation fog can be expected, and as the temperature rises with diurnal heating, the wind speed will increase as well and lift the fog into a low-level layer of stratus clouds.

options.label: D
options.text: Advection fog can be expected, and as the temperature rises with diurnal heating, the wind speed will increase as well and lift the fog into a low-level layer of stratus clouds.

correct_answer.text: Orographic fog can be expected, and as the temperature rises with diurnal heating, the fog is likely to lift into a cloud.

explanation: The destination at 700 ft on a ridge is in fog, while the lower aerodrome just to the west has a cloud base about 500 ft above it at about the same height. The westerly flow is lifted up the ridge and the cloud sits on high ground (orographic fog). As the day warms and the cloud base rises, the fog lifts into low cloud.

question: Refer to figure 050-166 What type of lightning is represented in figure 1?

options.label: A
options.text: Cloud to cloud

options.label: B
options.text: Cloud to ground

options.label: C
options.text: Intracloud

options.label: D
options.text: Cloud to air

correct_answer.text: Intracloud

explanation: In figure 050-166, figure 1 shows a discharge within a single cloud, which is intracloud lightning (the most common type).

question: What kind of turbulence can you expect in the vicinity of an airfield where a couple of buildings can be found?

options.label: A
options.text: Thermal turbulence

options.label: B
options.text: Shear turbulence

options.label: C
options.text: Mechanical turbulence

options.label: D
options.text: Aerodynamic turbulence

correct_answer.text: Mechanical turbulence

explanation: Buildings disturb the airflow and create eddies downwind of them. That is mechanical turbulence.

question: Refer to figure 050-237 You plan to take off from the marked aerodrome on Tuesday, 23rd April, 10:00 UTC. The following METAR was issued on 22nd April: 222100Z 26010KT 9999 BKN015 Q0995 Considering the information contained in the METAR, which of the offered options is most probable on the morning of the flight?

options.label: A
options.text: A depression is forming on the front to the west and cloud and rain can be expected as it develops.

options.label: B
options.text: The depression centred at 38°N, 004°E (994 hPa) is moving rapidly west; northerly winds should be expected at the aerodrome.

options.label: C
options.text: Radiation fog can be expected to form at the aerodrome in the early morning as the wind decreases.

options.label: D
options.text: The depression centred at 54°N, 013°W (992 hPa) is moving rapidly south; southerly winds should be expected at the aerodrome.

correct_answer.text: A depression is forming on the front to the west and cloud and rain can be expected as it develops.

explanation: Look in figure 050-237 for the front to the west of the aerodrome. With a moderate SW wind and broken cloud, radiation fog is unlikely, and a wave depression forming on that front is likely to bring cloud and rain by morning.

question: Refer to figure 050-97 Which figure in the attached diagram represents the typical jet stream flow patterns in July?
explanation: In July the subtropical jet and polar-front jet shift north and weaken, and the tropical easterly jet appears over India and Africa. Figure 3 shows that summer pattern.

question: Refer to figure 050-95 Which figure represents a "WARM OCCLUSION"?
explanation: In a warm occlusion, the air behind the cold front is warmer than the cold air ahead of the warm front. The cold front therefore rides up over the warm front, and the cold front aloft lies behind (to the rear of) the surface front. In figure 050-95 this is figure 2.

question: Which of the following cloud types is found at high level?

options.label: A
options.text: ST

options.label: B
options.text: SC

options.label: C
options.text: CS

options.label: D
options.text: AC

correct_answer.text: CS

explanation: CS (cirrostratus) is a high-level cloud. ST and SC are low clouds and AC is a mid-level cloud.

question: Refer to figure 050-33 The arrows labeled "V" represent the mean tracks of tropical revolving storms which occur mainly from:

options.label: A
options.text: May to November and are called Willy Willys

options.label: B
options.text: December to April and are called cyclones

options.label: C
options.text: May to November and are called typhoons

options.label: D
options.text: December to April and are called hurricanes

correct_answer.text: December to April and are called cyclones

explanation: Arrows V in figure 050-33 mark the South Indian Ocean or Australian region. Tropical revolving storms there occur in the southern summer (December to April) and are called cyclones.

question: What average geographical latitude is assumed for the zone of the travelling frontal depressions?
explanation: Travelling frontal depressions form along the polar front, which lies at about 60° latitude on average in this question bank's figures (about 40–60°).

question: A pilot is choosing an airport for arrival and looks for a runway, where the RVR is at least 550 m. The following METARs are valid for arrival time. Consider all other criteria for landing to each airport and choose the appropriate airport. EGKK 191050Z 09002KT 0200 FZFG R08R/0350 R08L/0500 VV001 M02/M03 Q1008 WS RWY08R EGLF 191050Z 07003KT 0200 FZFG R06/0700D VV001 M03/M03 Q1008 EGGW 191050Z 08004KT 0200 FZFG R08/0300U VV001 M02/M02 Q1007 EGLL 191050Z 09002KT 0100 FZFG R09L/0300U R09R/0500U VV001 M02/M02 Q1008

options.label: A
options.text: EGKK

options.label: B
options.text: EGGW

options.label: C
options.text: EGLL

options.label: D
options.text: EGLF

correct_answer.text: EGLF

explanation: EGLF reports R06/0700D (700 m, ≥ 550 m). Each of the others has an RVR below 550 m, and EGKK also has wind shear on runway 08R. Only EGLF meets the requirement.

question: At what maximum height can you expect Cb clouds around the equator and the tropic of cancer?
explanation: In the tropics the tropopause is high (about 16–18 km), so Cb tops can reach around 50 000 ft.

question: Vertical development clouds can contain both ice crystals and supercooled water droplets. Within what temperature range can you expect there to be significant amounts of both (as opposed to one type dominating)?

options.label: C
options.text: 0 °C and -15 °C

explanation: In this question bank, cloud between about −15 °C and −40 °C contains significant amounts of both ice crystals and supercooled droplets. Warmer than −15 °C supercooled droplets dominate, and colder than −40 °C the cloud is almost entirely ice.

question: An aircraft is parked outside and the crew arrives to the aircraft for an early morning flight. Since the night was clear and freezing cold, what is the crew likely to observe on the aircraft?

options.label: A
options.text: The convective cooling of the surface air sitting on the land overnight could lead to vapour sublimation on the fuselage.

options.label: B
options.text: The overnight radiative cooling of the land and fuselage surface may have caused hoar frost to form, covering the aircraft.

options.label: C
options.text: The sub-zero air temperature has probably created supercooled water droplets, which have formed clear ice on the aircraft.

options.label: D
options.text: The aircraft is likely to be covered in a hard layer of rime ice due to vapour sublimation.

correct_answer.text: The overnight radiative cooling of the land and fuselage surface may have caused hoar frost to form, covering the aircraft.

explanation: On a clear, cold night the aircraft surfaces cool by radiation below the frost point. Water vapour deposits directly as ice crystals, forming hoar frost over the aircraft, which must be removed before flight.
